title: How do you work out a yearly growth rate over several years?
description: Growth rates over several years: a quick way to do this case calculation in your head, with a worked example.
hook: Guess a round yearly rate, compound it over the number of years, compare with the actual end value and adjust. Never divide the total growth by the number of years, because growth compounds: each year builds on a bigger base, so the simple average always overstates the yearly rate.
body:
The method: guess, test, adjust

Revenue grew from $100M to $121M in two years. What was the growth rate each year?
  1. Total growth is 21%. Do not halve it: that gives 10.5%, which is too high.
  2. Guess a round rate. Try 10%.
  3. Test it: 1.1 × 1.1 = 1.21. That matches.
  4. Answer: 10% a year.

The halving error is small here, but it grows with the period and the rate. Over five years, revenue going from $50M to $80M is not 60% ÷ 5 = 12% a year; it is 1.6^(1/5) − 1 = 9.9%. This yearly rate is the CAGR, the compound annual growth rate.

How to say it in the interview

"That's 21% in total, but it compounds, so I won't just halve it. Let me try 10%: 1.1 times 1.1 is 1.21. That matches, so about 10% a year. If the market is growing at 5%, the client has been taking share."

Showing the check is what makes the answer convincing. The comparison at the end is what makes it useful.

A table to guess from

Memorise a few growth factors and you can find most rates in one step.

Yearly rateAfter 2 yearsAfter 3 yearsAfter 5 years
5%1.101.161.28
10%1.211.331.61
15%1.321.522.01
20%1.441.732.49

Example: sales grew from $40M to $60M in three years, a factor of 1.5. The table says 10% gives 1.33 and 15% gives 1.52, so the answer is just under 15%. The exact figure is 14.5%. For an interview, "just under 15% a year" is the right level of precision.

The 5-year column also gives you a feel for the rule of 72: 15% a year roughly doubles in five years, and 72 ÷ 15 = 4.8.

Forecasting forward

To project the same rate for another year, multiply the latest figure: $121M × 1.1 = $133.1M. Do not add another $10M, which was the first year's increase on a smaller base. Each year's increase is bigger than the last.

For several years at an awkward rate, step through it. $200M growing at 8% a year: year 1 is $216M, year 2 is about $233M, year 3 is about $252M.

Common mistakes

  • Dividing total growth by the years. It always overstates the yearly rate.
  • Adding yearly rates to get a total. Three years at 10% is +33%, not +30%.
  • Mixing annual and cumulative. Say which one you mean: "21% over two years, 10% a year."
  • Ignoring the benchmark. 10% growth is strong in a flat market and weak in one growing 20%. Ask for the market growth rate.

Practice

1. Sales went from $50M to $72M over two years. What was the yearly growth rate?

Show the answer

72 ÷ 50 = 1.44. From the table, 1.2 × 1.2 = 1.44, so 20% a year.

2. A market grew from $50M to $90M over four years. Roughly what is the CAGR?

Show the answer

The factor is 1.8. 1.15⁴ = 1.75 and 1.16⁴ = 1.81, so about 16% a year (15.8% exactly). Averaging, 80% ÷ 4 = 20%, would be well off.

3. A $200M business grows 8% a year. What is it worth in revenue after three years?

Show the answer

$200M → $216M → $233M → about $252M. Check: 1.08³ = 1.26, and $200M × 1.26 = $252M.
